overview: Alwa’s capital, Soba, lay on the Blue Nile in what is now Sudan. Kings and church leaders shared this city with people who built, traded and prepared food. Its buried buildings and everyday objects let us look beyond royal history.

periods.title: A capital develops
periods.summary: Soba developed as a major town in the fifth and sixth centuries. Alwa was one of the medieval Nubian kingdoms, distinct from Makuria and Nobadia. The map begins its coverage at 600.

periods.title: A city with distant connections
periods.summary: A tenth-century visitor described gardens, monasteries, churches and a Muslim district. Imported glass helps archaeologists trace connections with Egypt and the Middle East.

periods.title: Changing districts and an uncertain ending
periods.summary: Parts of Soba were already ruined before the thirteenth century, while other buildings remained in use. Archaeology reveals uneven change across the city, rather than one securely dated moment when all life stopped.

periods.title: Ruins and reused building materials
periods.summary: Later tradition associates Soba’s defeat with 1504. In the nineteenth century, bricks from its ruins were taken for buildings in Khartoum. These are different episodes in the site’s history.

periods.title: Discovering and discussing Soba
periods.summary: Excavation, scientific analysis and conversations with residents reveal different aspects of the past. Recent work has also involved local schoolchildren and Sudanese students and researchers.

sections.title: Food, families and the work behind a meal

items.text: At Soba, Deposit 7 in trench 1/GN contained six lower grinding stones and fourteen handheld grinders. Large basin-shaped stones paired with disc-shaped grinders probably supported processing such as turning grain into flour. The investigators also suggest smaller tools served smaller tasks. Making a meal could start with an arm workout: no button marked “blend”. The exact foods processed on each stone remain uncertain.

Researchers examining Soba samples reported charred broomcorn millet and grape seeds. The samples came from contexts including vessel fills and ash-bearing deposits. These tiny remains add plants to the story told by pots and grinding stones. Grapes do not automatically mean wine, and the preliminary report does not reconstruct a complete family menu. Many uncharred remains were considered modern contamination.

A 2024 study examined tooth enamel from fourteen people buried at Soba’s Cemetery OS. Chemical traces formed during childhood point to heavy reliance on foods from a plant group that includes millet and sorghum, and possibly products from animals eating similar plants. Teeth can preserve clues to childhood meals, but they cannot hand us a recipe or identify every ingredient.

Comparisons between people, animals and regional water chemistry led the same researchers to suggest seasonal movement between the Nile valley and nearby grasslands. In their interpretation, some herders may have travelled with family members, including children. This is a possible explanation of the chemical evidence, not a recovered travel diary or proof that every Soba household lived the same way.

sections.title: Building, making and connecting a city

items.text: In trench 1/OS, excavators found mud-brick walls and evidence that an open area later became a roofed room. An impression left by a palm log helped identify its roof supports. These remains show a space changing over time; they do not identify the household, room occupants or purpose of every activity inside.

Another excavation on Mound OS found lime deposits and kiln remains. Radiocarbon samples place the production deposit around the early eleventh century. Making building materials left traces as well as constructing the finished buildings: the city required skilled work behind the scenes.

A 2023 study tested twenty-three glass beads from Soba. Their chemistry linked most samples to glass made in northern India, with others connected to Egypt and the Middle East. Small ornaments could therefore participate in enormous exchange networks. A bead’s ingredients can suggest its origin, but cannot tell us every stop on its journey or the identity of its wearer.

Excavations in 2019 to 2022 recovered glass fragments and an object identified as a cosmetic bottle. Analysis of thirty fragments linked their glass to production in Egypt, the Levant and the Middle East. Glass served purposes beyond jewellery, including vessels and windows. The bottle’s label is not a chemical identification of its original contents, and these finds do not prove every home had glass windows.

The project begun in 2019 used magnetic surveys to detect buried structures, then tested interpretations by excavating selected places. In Area F, the survey suggested closely packed mud-brick houses and irregular streets. This reveals a neighbourhood’s layout without digging up every square metre, although a magnetic pattern still needs interpretation and cannot name the family living behind a wall.

sections.title: The past in homes and classrooms

items.text: Interviews reported in 2021 found that some modern Soba households kept old grinding stones and displayed pottery fragments. Women connected such objects with memories of family homes. An archaeological object can become part of somebody’s living room, not only a museum collection. Modern reuse does not prove an unbroken custom stretching back to Alwa.

In December 2022, workshops in Soba schools asked children to discuss archaeology and draw their ideas about the past. Pictures included brick houses, water containers and objects used at home. Researchers noted that classroom discussion and textbooks influenced the drawings. Children were contributing their own ideas, while the pictures remained modern interpretations rather than illustrations made by medieval residents.

During research in early 2023, women in Soba and the Mahas region discussed clothing, food and homes in interviews and meetings, including conversations over coffee and sweets. Researchers compared local traditions instead of assuming one uniform Sudanese way of life. Their work records modern women’s knowledge; it does not make every present-day resident a direct descendant of medieval Soba’s population.

ending.text: Later accounts link Soba’s conquest by Sennar’s first ruler to 1504. Excavation reveals districts abandoned at different times, with some buildings still used in the thirteenth century. Alwa’s final political transition remains uncertain. The map’s 1530 endpoint is not a verified fall year, and collapse did not mean everyone disappeared.
